questions.prompt: A stack follows which access discipline?
questions.explanation: The most recently pushed element is the first one popped. Push and pop both act on the same end, the top, and both run in O(1).

questions.prompt: Which data structure is the natural choice for checking whether the brackets in an expression are balanced?
questions.explanation: Push each opening bracket and pop on each closing one, checking the pair matches. The last opened bracket must be the first closed — exactly LIFO order.

questions.prompt: A queue follows which access discipline?
questions.explanation: Elements are removed in the order they were added: enqueue at the rear, dequeue from the front. This models real-world waiting lines and breadth-first processing.

questions.prompt: Why is a circular queue preferred over a linear array queue with front and rear indices?

options.text: It allows random access to any element
It reuses vacated front slots instead of wasting them
It removes the need for a rear index

questions.explanation: In a linear array, dequeued front slots become unusable and the queue drifts toward the end. Wrapping the rear index around with modulo arithmetic reclaims that space.

questions.prompt: Which structure is used to evaluate a postfix (reverse Polish) expression?
questions.explanation: Push operands, and on each operator pop the top two, apply it, and push the result. The final value left on the stack is the answer.

questions.prompt: Which run-time mechanism is directly modelled by a stack?

options.text: The function call stack that supports recursion

questions.explanation: Each call pushes an activation record and returning pops it, so the most recent call finishes first. Deep recursion can overflow this stack.

questions.prompt: A queue can be implemented using two stacks. What is the amortised cost per operation?
questions.explanation: Enqueue pushes onto an inbox stack. Dequeue pops from an outbox stack, refilling it by reversing the inbox only when empty. Each element is moved between stacks at most once, so cost is O(1) amortised.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes a deque from an ordinary queue?

options.text: Insertion and removal are allowed at both ends
It only allows removal from the middle
It has a fixed capacity of two

questions.explanation: A double-ended queue supports push and pop at both front and rear, so it can behave as a stack, a queue, or both. It is the structure behind the sliding-window maximum pattern.

questions.prompt: How does a priority queue differ from an ordinary FIFO queue?

options.text: It dequeues the most recently added element
It dequeues the highest-priority element rather than the oldest

questions.explanation: Order of removal depends on a priority key, not arrival time. It is usually backed by a heap, giving O(log n) insert and extract rather than the O(1) of a plain queue.

questions.prompt: A program crashes with a stack overflow. Which is the most likely cause?

options.text: Allocating a large array on the heap
Unbounded recursion with no reachable base case

questions.explanation: Each recursive call consumes a stack frame; without a base case the frames accumulate until the call stack's fixed space is exhausted. Large heap allocations fail differently, as out-of-memory.
